blocks.h2: Silicosis built this city's safety culture
blocks.html:
Potters' rot — silicosis — was the Potteries' industrial disease for two centuries, and modern ceramic works run the controls that history bought: extraction and wet methods first, FFP3 where fettling, dry finishing and material handling still make dust, fit-tested properly, with health surveillance behind it. A ceramics buyer asking for 'dust masks' should be handed the terminology page and FFP3 — this is the city where the difference was learned the hard way.

The kiln side runs on EN 407 contact-heat thinking: ware, cranks and kiln furniture hold heat long after the ovens open, and the burns are contact burns — gloves with real contact ratings and forearm cover, in a works culture that treats 'still warm' as the default assumption.

faq.q: What PPE is needed for ceramics work?
faq.a: By process: FFP3 respiratory protection where clay and glaze dusts form (silica is the historic hazard), EN 407 contact-heat gloves at kilns and ware handling, nitrile and aprons for glaze work, eye protection at fettling and spraying, and washable workwear in rotation. Extraction and wet methods lead; PPE covers the remainder.

faq.q: Why is silica dust a problem in the Potteries?
faq.a: Clay bodies and glaze materials contain crystalline silica, and dry processes — fettling, finishing, material handling — release respirable dust that causes silicosis, the disease that defined the industry's history. Modern works control it with extraction, wet working and fit-tested FFP3, backed by health surveillance.

Glass processing is where the ISO 13997 cut letters stop being abstract: handling float sheet, offcuts and breakage calls for level D as a floor and F where sheets are large, with grip coatings that hold smooth heavy material and cuff length that covers the wrist — the same slide-down-the-carry injury logic as the glazing trade, at line speed. Sleeve protection for arms and aprons for the body follow wherever manual handling meets sheet edges.

The hot end inverts it: forming and lehr work is radiant-and-contact heat territory — heavy natural-fibre or FR layers, EN 407 gauntlets, and the quiet rule toughening lines teach everyone: glass out of the process looks cool long before it is.
